title: Summarizing Decisions in Spoken Meetings
research_question: How effectively can decision-related utterances in multi-party meetings be clustered by decision and summarized using dialogue-act-level or token-level supervised and unsupervised methods?
methodology: The work uses the AMI meeting corpus and assumes decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified. It first clusters decision-related utterances belonging to the same decision using TF-IDF or LDA-based unsupervised methods and supervised classifiers, then generates extractive summaries at the dialogue-act or token level with optional discourse context. Cluster quality is evaluated with clustering measures and summary quality with ROUGE against human decision abstracts.

key_findings.finding: Decision-related dialogue acts can be distributed and interleaved across a meeting, motivating an explicit clustering stage before decision summarization.
Supervised clustering performs better than the reported unsupervised LDA clustering on B-cubed F1, although the LDA method remains competitive for downstream summary quality.
With automatically produced clusters, an unsupervised LDA-based clustering pipeline can yield decision-summary quality comparable to the supervised clustering alternative.

When true decision clusters are supplied, supervised token-level summarization with discourse context achieves the strongest reported supervised configuration and approaches the paper's extractive upper bound more closely than automatic-cluster conditions.
The AMI data are scenario-driven four-person design-team meetings rather than authentic enterprise email or chat logs.
The task summarizes decisions but does not provide structured evaluation of assignee, deadline, condition, negation, modality, or exact argument evidence spans.

limitations: The corpus consists of scenario-driven spoken design meetings rather than naturally occurring enterprise email or chat.
The system assumes that decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified, so decision detection itself is outside the evaluated pipeline.
The output is decision summarization rather than structured extraction of action, assignee, deadline, condition, or decision arguments.
Implicit and group assignees are not defined as dedicated annotation targets.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not separately annotated or evaluated.
ROUGE-based summary scoring does not enforce exact evidence spans for individual structured arguments.
Some clustering stopping thresholds are manually selected.
raw_claims: The work targets concise summaries of individual decisions made during meetings.
Decision-related dialogue acts associated with one decision may be separated by other discussion.
The experiments use the AMI meeting corpus.
AMI contains scenario-driven meetings involving four participants playing design-team roles.
The experiments assume decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified.
The pipeline separately studies clustering and summarization.
Both unsupervised and supervised clustering approaches are evaluated.
Both dialogue-act-level and token-level summary selection are investigated.
Human-written decision abstracts provide the summary reference.
Automatic clustering substantially constrains downstream summary quality compared with true decision clusters.
ROUGE is used to assess generated decision summaries.
